rationale: B wins because it keeps the same three real story shapes without stepping on a landmine. A's FedNow angle, "FedNow gets its first big merchant-payments use case," invents "first" and "big" from a fact set that gives no volume and no named merchant. B's version, "FedNow gets a merchant-facing on-ramp through Plaid's 12,000 bank connections," is the adult phrasing: still interesting, less likely to get the founder corrected by the first infrastructure reporter who opens the email.
gaps_in_A: "FedNow gets its first big merchant-payments use case" is overclaimed. The update says Pay by Bank uses FedNow rails; it does not prove first, big, live volume, or merchant scale.
"evidence about whether the rails are reaching commercial scale" gets ahead of the facts. No volume, named merchant, or adoption data was supplied.
"a card-network or merchant-association response" is a useful proof item, but it is more wishlist than required proof for the launch angle; named merchant and fee schedule matter more.
gaps_in_B: "covering the card networks' interchange economics and who is trying to erode them" is syntactically sloppy enough to briefly imply the reporter is trying to erode card networks. That sentence needed one more pass.

"this is an early merchant-payments use of them" is plausible but still an inference. Better to say it is a launch using FedNow for merchant payments, then require proof of whether it is early or meaningful.

The set is clean, but it underplays the private-company angle. Plaid being privately held is not a story by itself, but it changes what proof reporters can realistically demand and what financials they will not get.
